Q010.L1t: India has one of the largest populations of internet users in the world in absolute terms.
Q010.L2t: Survey-based estimates of internet use in India, such as those cited by the World Bank and ITU, count people who accessed the internet within the past three months.
Q010.L3t: By 2017 roughly a quarter of India's population was online, meaning about one in four people, which is well above a tenth but well short of a third.
Q010.L4t: In 2017 about a quarter of India's population, roughly 26 percent, had used the internet in the previous three months.
Q010.L2f: The three-month usage measure for India is collected only from urban households, and rural residents are not counted in the national estimate.
Q010.L3f: In 2017 only about one in ten Indians had access to the internet, since mobile data was still very expensive and limited to a small urban elite.
Q010.L4f: In 2017 only about 11 percent of India's population had used the internet in the previous three months.

Q011.L1t: Corporal punishment in schools has been a widely documented concern in South Asian education systems.
Q011.L2t: The Young Lives longitudinal study followed cohorts of children in India and collected data on their school experiences, including punishment by teachers.
Q011.L3t: The Young Lives survey found that the large majority of eight-year-olds in India, roughly three out of four, reported being physically punished by teachers in the past week.
Q011.L4t: About 78 percent of eight-year-old children in India reported physical punishment by teachers in the past week in 2009.
Q011.L2f: The Young Lives study in India was conducted only in private schools, and its punishment questions were asked of teachers rather than of the children.
Q011.L3f: Young Lives data from 2009 showed that only a minority of eight-year-olds in India, around one in three, reported physical punishment by teachers in the past week.
Q011.L4f: About 38 percent of eight-year-old children in India reported physical punishment by teachers in the past week in 2009.

Q012.L1t: Development economists have debated many strategies for reducing poverty in developing countries, including growth-first and redistributive approaches.
Q012.L2t: The redistribution-with-growth approach was popularized in the 1970s, notably by the World Bank, and aimed to raise the incomes of the poor through asset and investment-focused measures.
Q012.L3t: Redistribution with growth focuses on shifting assets and investment toward the poor, such as land, education and the tax system, rather than regulating wages in the labor market.
Q012.L4t: Minimum wage legislation is the item that is not part of the redistribution-with-growth approach.
Q012.L2f: The redistribution-with-growth approach was developed in the 1990s as a rejection of any government role in the economy, and it relied solely on market liberalization.
Q012.L3f: Redistribution with growth is defined by its reliance on wage regulation and spending programs, and it explicitly avoids using the tax system to move resources from rich to poor.
Q012.L4f: Progressive taxation is the item that is not part of the redistribution-with-growth approach.

Q013.L1t: Religiosity varies widely across European countries, and France is often cited as one of the more secular nations in Western Europe.
Q013.L2t: Pew and Gallup surveys have long found that France ranks among the least religious countries in Europe, with a large share of adults identifying as nonreligious.
Q013.L3t: In the 2019 survey, only a minority of French respondents, well under half and closer to one in three than to one in two, said God plays an important role in their life.
Q013.L4t: The share of French people who say God plays an important role in their life is roughly one in three, about thirty-one percent.
Q013.L2f: Surveys have shown France to be one of the most devout countries in Europe, with religious attendance and belief rising steadily in recent decades.
Q013.L3f: In the 2019 survey, French respondents were split almost evenly, with about half saying God plays an important role in their life and half saying it does not.
Q013.L4f: The share of French people who say God plays an important role in their life is about half, roughly fifty-one percent.

Q014.L1t: Saudi Arabia is one of the world's largest military spenders and its defense budget is closely tied to oil revenue.
Q014.L2t: Saudi Arabia has ranked among the top five countries in the world for military expenditure in recent years, buying large quantities of imported weapons.
Q014.L3t: In 2017 Saudi military spending was a very large fraction of national output, higher than the roughly six percent level, putting it in the double digits and well above the global average of about two percent.
Q014.L4t: Saudi Arabia spent about ten percent of its GDP on the military in 2017.
Q014.L2f: Saudi Arabia's military spending has fallen sharply in recent years, and the country relies mostly on domestically produced weapons rather than imports.
Q014.L3f: In 2017 Saudi military spending was a moderate share of national output, a bit more than twice the global average of about two percent and below the double-digit range.
Q014.L4f: Saudi Arabia spent about six percent of its GDP on the military in 2017.

Q015.L1t: Perceptions of corruption in public institutions are commonly measured through cross-country opinion surveys such as the Global Corruption Barometer.
Q015.L2t: Ethiopia has been governed by a dominant ruling coalition for decades, with a political party system in which opposition parties hold very few seats.
Q015.L3t: In the 2013 survey, Ethiopians were comparatively unlikely to describe political parties as corrupt, with the share being a minority of under a third of respondents, far lower than in most other countries surveyed.
Q015.L4t: The share of Ethiopians who think political parties are corrupt in 2013 was low, about twenty-four percent.
Q015.L2f: Ethiopia held multiparty elections in 2013 that were widely reported to have been won by a competitive opposition coalition.
Q015.L3f: In the 2013 survey, Ethiopians were among the most likely in the world to view political parties as corrupt, with a large majority of respondents, well over three quarters, saying so.
Q015.L4f: The share of Ethiopians who think political parties are corrupt in 2013 was very high, about eighty-four percent.

Q016.L1t: Corporal punishment in schools is a documented concern in many low- and middle-income countries, and longitudinal studies such as Young Lives track children's experiences of it.
Q016.L2t: The Young Lives study followed children in Ethiopia, India, Peru and Vietnam, and collected self-reports of school discipline from children around age 8.
Q016.L3t: In the Young Lives data for Ethiopia, the share of 8-year-olds reporting teacher physical punishment in the past week was clearly more than one in three but well under half.
Q016.L4t: About thirty-eight percent of Ethiopian 8-year-olds reported being physically punished by teachers in the past week in 2009.
Q016.L2f: The Young Lives study surveyed Ethiopian children only at age 15 and did not collect any self-reports about discipline at school.
Q016.L3f: In the Young Lives data for Ethiopia, a clear majority of 8-year-olds, well over half but under four in five, reported teacher physical punishment in the past week.
Q016.L4f: About fifty-eight percent of Ethiopian 8-year-olds reported being physically punished by teachers in the past week in 2009.

Q017.L1t: School violence, including physical fighting among adolescents, is monitored internationally through standardized student health surveys.
Q017.L2t: The Global School-based Student Health Survey and similar tools ask students aged 13-15 whether they were in physical fights during the previous 12 months.
Q017.L3t: In the 2015 US survey data, the share of students aged 13-15 reporting at least one physical fight at school in the past year was well above one in five and below half.
Q017.L4t: About thirty-five percent of US children aged 13-15 reported being in a physical fight at school in the past 12 months as of 2015.
Q017.L2f: The US school-based youth survey on fighting only asks about incidents during the past 30 days and never covers a 12-month period.
Q017.L3f: In the 2015 US survey data, only a small minority of students aged 13-15, roughly one in seven, reported any physical fight at school in the past year.
Q017.L4f: About fifteen percent of US children aged 13-15 reported being in a physical fight at school in the past 12 months as of 2015.

Q018.L1t: Petty corruption in public services is measured in cross-country surveys such as Transparency International's Global Corruption Barometer.
Q018.L2t: The 2017 Global Corruption Barometer for Asia Pacific asked respondents whether they had paid a bribe in the previous 12 months to access services like education, health, police, and permits.
Q018.L3t: In the 2017 Asia Pacific barometer, India's reported bribery rate was well above half of service users but clearly below the near-universal levels, sitting at roughly two in three.
Q018.L4t: About sixty-nine percent of survey respondents from India reported having paid a bribe in the last year to access public services as of 2017.
Q018.L2f: The 2017 Global Corruption Barometer for Asia Pacific only surveyed urban residents of national capitals and excluded any questions about actually paying bribes.
Q018.L3f: In the 2017 Asia Pacific barometer, India's bribery rate was extremely high, with nearly nine in ten service users reporting having paid a bribe.
Q018.L4f: About eighty-nine percent of survey respondents from India reported having paid a bribe in the last year to access public services as of 2017.

Q019.L1t: HIV/AIDS has caused tens of millions of deaths worldwide since the epidemic began in the early 1980s.
Q019.L2t: Most people living with HIV are adults, and sub-Saharan Africa accounts for the large majority of AIDS-related deaths.
Q019.L3t: HIV is mainly transmitted sexually, through blood and from mother to child, and after infection it typically takes years to progress to AIDS, so deaths concentrate among people infected as young adults who are in their sexually active years.
Q019.L4t: The highest HIV/AIDS death rate is among adults in the prime working ages, roughly 15 to 49.
Q019.L2f: HIV was first identified as a distinct virus in the 1960s, and antiretroviral therapy has been available since the early 1970s.
Q019.L3f: Because HIV progression is very slow and most people infected in adulthood survive for several decades, AIDS deaths are concentrated among people who are already past middle age.
Q019.L4f: The highest HIV/AIDS death rate is among people older than fifty.

Q030.L1t: Dwight Eisenhower was a five-star general in World War II before serving two terms as US president from 1953 to 1961.
Q030.L2t: Eisenhower delivered his farewell address on television on January 17, 1961, a few days before leaving office.
Q030.L3t: Eisenhower warned that a permanent, large arms industry joined with a huge military establishment was a new feature of American life, and that government must guard against it acquiring unwarranted influence in the councils of government.
Q030.L4t: He argued that the arms industry and military spending had gained undue political influence over government, which threatened democratic control.
Q030.L2f: Eisenhower's farewell address was delivered in 1965 to a joint session of Congress, several years after he had left office.
Q030.L3f: Eisenhower argued in the speech that the profit motive of capitalism was itself the underlying driver of wars, and that markets pushed nations into conflict.
Q030.L4f: He argued that capitalist profit-seeking was the main cause of armed conflict.

Q031.L1t: Diplomacy is the conduct of relations between states, traditionally carried out through envoys, ambassadors and negotiations.
Q031.L2t: In US foreign policy studies, the term is used for a form of diplomacy that sits outside the executive branch's usual channels.
Q031.L3t: In the study of US foreign policy, direct diplomacy refers to the legislative branch, not the executive, engaging with foreign counterparts itself, for example through congressional delegations visiting other countries.
Q031.L4t: Direct diplomacy means members of Congress negotiating directly with foreign governments.
Q031.L2f: The term direct diplomacy was coined during the 1648 Peace of Westphalia and has been used in the same way ever since.
Q031.L3f: The key feature of direct diplomacy is that the top leaders of states sit down together in person, without ambassadors or intermediaries acting for them.
Q031.L4f: Direct diplomacy means face-to-face meetings between state leaders.

Q032.L1t: The Clinton Administration's foreign policy followed the post-Cold War era's emphasis on engagement and enlargement of democratic and market-oriented states.
Q032.L2t: After the Soviet collapse, Russia underwent a turbulent transition away from central planning in the 1990s, involving privatization and large Western advisory and financial involvement.
Q032.L3t: The Clinton Administration backed IMF and Western aid packages and advisers for Russia that were tied to privatization, price liberalization and other market-oriented reforms.
Q032.L4t: The Clinton Administration actively pushed Russia toward a market economy.
Q032.L2f: Russia's transition in the 1990s was a gradual, carefully planned process in which the state kept firm control of prices and industry throughout the decade.
Q032.L3f: Clinton Administration officials worked to slow down or block Russian privatization and price liberalization, and they pressed international lenders to withhold aid that was tied to reform.
Q032.L4f: The Clinton Administration obstructed Russia's shift to a market economy.

Q033.L1t: Oil is a strategically vital commodity that has shaped relations between the United States and many countries, especially in the Middle East.
Q033.L2t: The 1973 Arab oil embargo caused fuel shortages and price spikes in the United States and prompted lasting changes in American energy and foreign policy.
Q033.L3t: Oil's influence on U.S. policy often operates through trade, sanctions, pricing, alliances and aid, which are economic tools instead of battlefield force.
Q033.L4t: The role of oil shows that economic instruments are becoming more important in foreign policy.
Q033.L2f: The 1973 Arab oil embargo had almost no effect on U.S. fuel prices or supplies and left American energy policy unchanged.
Q033.L3f: U.S. policy on oil has been carried out almost entirely through armed force and basing, while economic tools like sanctions, trade and pricing have played a negligible role.
Q033.L4f: The role of oil shows that military superiority is the most important thing in foreign policy.

Q034.L1t: Scholars of international relations often study how security and economic development relate to one another within states.
Q034.L2t: Historically, wars and external threats have changed how states raise revenue, organize bureaucracies and distribute power.
Q034.L3t: When a state faces security threats, its leaders tend to concentrate political and economic authority in the central government, which can distort resource allocation and undermine the conditions for development.
Q034.L4t: Threats to the state lead to centralization of political and economic power, and that centralization harms development.
Q034.L2f: Historically, external threats have had no bearing on how states raise revenue, organize bureaucracies or distribute power.
Q034.L3f: Security threats cause populations and elites to turn against private property and markets and demand collective ownership of the economy, which then shapes the state's development path.
Q034.L4f: Threats to the state encourage socialism, which is why development is tied to security.

Q035.L1t: The Vietnam War was a major Cold War conflict in which the United States supported South Vietnam against communist North Vietnam.
Q035.L2t: The Gulf of Tonkin resolution was passed by Congress in August 1964, after reported attacks on US destroyers by North Vietnamese patrol boats.
Q035.L3t: The resolution authorised the President to take all necessary measures to repel armed attack and prevent further aggression, without requiring a formal declaration of war from Congress.
Q035.L4t: The resolution gave President Johnson broad legal authority to escalate US military involvement in Vietnam.
Q035.L2f: The Gulf of Tonkin resolution was passed by Congress in 1968, after the Tet Offensive had shocked the American public.
Q035.L3f: The resolution required the President to obtain Congressional approval before committing any further troops or launching any new military operations in Vietnam.
Q035.L4f: The resolution's significance was that it strengthened Congress's authority over how the Vietnam War was conducted.

Q036.L1t: Ronald Reagan was US president from 1981 to 1989, a period that saw the final phase of the Cold War.
Q036.L2t: Reagan's administration launched the Strategic Defense Initiative in 1983 and oversaw a large peacetime defence build-up.
Q036.L3t: The Soviet economy was already stagnating, and Reagan's first-term rise in US arms spending forced the Soviets to try to match it, straining their finances and overstretching their global commitments.
Q036.L4t: Scholars say he won the Cold War because his large military build-up pressured the Soviet Union into overextending itself.
Q036.L2f: Reagan's administration cancelled the Strategic Defense Initiative soon after announcing it in 1983.
Q036.L3f: Reagan cut US defence budgets sharply in his first term, which took pressure off Moscow and gave Soviet leaders room to carry out domestic reforms.
Q036.L4f: Scholars say he won the Cold War because he cut military spending, which gave the Soviet Union space to reform.

Q037.L1t: The American Revolution produced a new republic that rejected monarchy and set out to define its own place among the world's powers.
Q037.L2t: Many founders, including Thomas Jefferson, worried that empires historically tended toward tyranny and the loss of liberty.
Q037.L3t: Jefferson and other founders argued that an expanding republic built on self-government and liberty could escape the despotism of European empires, and so presented its growth as a spread of freedom.
Q037.L4t: They believed their empire would be an 'empire of liberty', with expansion serving freedom rather than tyranny.
Q037.L2f: After 1776 most American leaders opposed all territorial expansion and wanted the new republic to remain confined to the thirteen original states.
Q037.L3f: Founders held that the new empire would deliberately bring together peoples of many cultures and origins as equal citizens, and that this would set it apart from European empires.
Q037.L4f: They believed their new empire would be distinctive because it would be multi-cultural.

Q038.L1t: The end of the Cold War in 1989–1991 reshaped how states thought about international politics and the role of the United States.
Q038.L2t: President George H. W. Bush used the phrase 'New World Order' in speeches around the 1990–91 Gulf War, as the Soviet Union was fading.
Q038.L3t: Bush's usage emphasized the US leading other nations through collective action, democratic values and international institutions like the UN, rather than a purely economic or two-power arrangement.
Q038.L4t: The phrase meant a post-Cold War international order in which the United States led a democratic, cooperative internationalism.
Q038.L2f: The phrase 'New World Order' was first coined by Ronald Reagan in his 1984 re-election campaign to describe NAFTA negotiations.
Q038.L3f: Bush used the phrase mainly to announce a restructuring of trade rules, currency systems and investment regimes among the major economies after the Cold War.
Q038.L4f: The term meant a new global economic framework governing trade, finance and investment among nations.

Q039.L1t: The 'American Creed' is a concept in political culture describing shared ideals thought to unite Americans across their differences.
Q039.L2t: The term was popularized by Gunnar Myrdal and later Samuel Huntington, who used it to describe the core political values of American identity.
Q039.L3t: The Creed consists of ideals about the rights and self-reliance of citizens and rule by the people, so a system where one ruler holds unchecked power contradicts it.
Q039.L4t: Autocracy is not part of the American Creed, since it is rule by a single person and opposes the creed's democratic ideals.
Q039.L2f: The American Creed was formally written into the Constitution's preamble as a numbered list of five required national values.
Q039.L3f: The Creed's core ideals are generally described as order, hierarchy and obedience, and a value centered on freedom would be foreign to it.
Q039.L4f: Liberty is not part of the American Creed and is the item that does not belong.

Q050.L1t: Hydraulic systems in farm machinery transmit power through fluid, and fluid condition matters for reliable operation.
Q050.L2t: Water can enter a hydraulic system through condensation, worn seals or contaminated top-up fluid, causing corrosion and component wear.
Q050.L3t: Water does not mix with hydraulic oil and instead emulsifies with it, changing its appearance visibly when the oil is inspected.
Q050.L4t: A grayish, milky look to the fluid is the sign that water has contaminated it.
Q050.L2f: Water in a hydraulic system is harmless to pumps and valves and is normally absorbed fully by the oil without any change.
Q050.L3f: Water in hydraulic oil mainly lowers its viscosity, so the fluid becomes noticeably runny and loses its body when it is contaminated.
Q050.L4f: Excessive thinning of the fluid is the most likely sign that water is present in the hydraulic system.

Q051.L1t: Parking enforcement worldwide uses a range of tools, including fines, towing and physical restraints, to deter illegal parking.
Q051.L2t: Wheel-immobilizing devices for vehicles were first used in the United States in the 1950s as a way to deal with unpaid parking tickets.
Q051.L3t: The device police use is a large metal clamp that locks onto a wheel so the car cannot be driven, and it is named after the Colorado city where it first came into use.
Q051.L4t: The metal wheel-immobilizing device police use on repeat parking offenders is the Denver boot.
Q051.L2f: Wheel-immobilizing devices were first introduced in Europe in the 1990s and were originally made of hardened rubber rather than metal.
Q051.L3f: The device police use on repeat offenders is a tracking unit hidden in the vehicle that lets officers find and recover the car, rather than a clamp fitted to a wheel.
Q051.L4f: The device police use to immobilize the wheels of repeat parking offenders is LoJack.

Q052.L1t: Geometry classifies angles by their size, measured in degrees, and each kind has its own name.
Q052.L2t: Perpendicular lines are lines in the same plane that intersect each other at a single point.
Q052.L3t: Perpendicular lines meet so that each of the four angles they form measures exactly 90 degrees, which is a quarter of a full turn.
Q052.L4t: Two perpendicular lines form a right angle where they meet.
Q052.L2f: Perpendicular lines can never cross each other, because lines that intersect are always parallel in the same plane.
Q052.L3f: Perpendicular lines meet at an angle of less than 90 degrees, so the angle they form is smaller than a quarter turn.
Q052.L4f: Two perpendicular lines form an acute angle where they meet.

Q053.L1t: Fast food companies in the United States have long competed through memorable television advertising campaigns and catchphrases.
Q053.L2t: The 'Where's the beef?' slogan appeared in a television commercial in 1984 and became a popular catchphrase, even being used in that year's presidential campaign.
Q053.L3t: The ad showed an elderly woman looking at a burger with a huge bun and a tiny patty, and it was made for a chain whose founder, Dave Thomas, named it after his daughter.
Q053.L4t: Wendy's was the fast food chain that used the slogan 'Where's the beef?'
Q053.L2f: The 'Where's the beef?' commercial first aired in the 1960s and starred a cartoon mascot instead of real people.
Q053.L3f: The 'Where's the beef?' ad was made for a chain founded by Colonel Harland Sanders, whose fried chicken is sold in buckets and whose face is on the logo.
Q053.L4f: Kentucky Fried Chicken was the fast food chain that used the slogan 'Where's the beef?'

Q054.L1t: Remote controls are handheld devices that send commands wirelessly to electronics from across a room.
Q054.L2t: Most household remotes have a small LED at the front end and generally need to be pointed toward a receiver on the device.
Q054.L3t: Typical TV remotes use a line-of-sight LED that emits light just beyond the red end of the spectrum, which the eye cannot see, flashed in a coded on-off pattern.
Q054.L4t: The signal is encoded as a series of infrared pulses.
Q054.L2f: The first television remote controls appeared in the 1990s, after cable television became widespread.
Q054.L3f: A remote's LED emits light at wavelengths the human eye can see, which is why people can watch it flash when they press a button.
Q054.L4f: The remote encodes its signal in pulses of light that people can see, so that is the right answer.

Q055.L1t: English spelling contains many irregular patterns because the language borrowed words from many other languages.
Q055.L2t: The rule 'i before e, except after c' is a common memory aid, though it has many exceptions.
Q055.L3t: The word for health and cleanliness practices comes from the Greek goddess Hygieia and keeps the i before the e after the g.
Q055.L4t: The correctly spelled word is the one for cleanliness practices, spelled h-y-g-i-e-n-e.
Q055.L2f: The rule 'i before e, except after c' has no exceptions in standard English spelling.
Q055.L3f: In the word meaning 'from another country,' the i comes before the e, following the standard i-before-e pattern.
Q055.L4f: The correct spelling is the word meaning 'from another country,' with the i placed before the e.

Q056.L1t: Square roots and exponents are related operations that are taught together in arithmetic and algebra.
Q056.L2t: Squaring a number means multiplying it by itself.
Q056.L3t: Taking a square root and squaring are inverse operations, so applying one and then the other returns the number you started with.
Q056.L4t: The result is simply the original number, eighty-one.
Q056.L2f: Squaring a number means adding it to itself once.
Q056.L3f: Squaring the root of a number just means multiplying that root by three, so the root of nine gets tripled.
Q056.L4f: The answer is three times nine, the product of the root and three.

Q057.L1t: Teachers choose reading materials for many purposes, including building skills, covering content, and sustaining motivation.
Q057.L2t: Student engagement in reading is closely tied to motivation, which depends on how much learners care about what they are reading.
Q057.L3t: Students are most motivated to read and participate when the material connects with what they personally find interesting, which is a different factor from what the teacher needs to cover or from the difficulty of the text.
Q057.L4t: A teacher should choose texts on topics the students themselves find interesting.
Q057.L2f: Research shows student engagement in reading is unaffected by motivation and depends only on how long students spend on a text.
Q057.L3f: Students engage most when each text is chosen to match the lesson's stated goals, because clear alignment with what is to be learned is what draws learners in.
Q057.L4f: A teacher should choose texts according to the instructional objectives to best encourage engagement.

Q058.L1t: Heat is energy that moves from warmer regions to cooler ones, and it can be studied in solids, liquids, gases, and empty space.
Q058.L2t: The three recognized ways heat moves are named for how energy travels through a material, through moving fluid, or through electromagnetic waves.
Q058.L3t: Induction is the term for generating an electric current or magnetic effect by a changing magnetic field, which is an electromagnetic process and not a way of moving thermal energy.
Q058.L4t: Induction is the one that is not a method of heat transfer.
Q058.L2f: Heat transfer by the three standard methods only happens in solids and cannot occur through liquids, gases, or a vacuum.
Q058.L3f: Conduction involves only electric current flowing through wires and has nothing to do with thermal energy moving between touching objects, so it is not a way heat moves.
Q058.L4f: Conduction is the one that is not a method of heat transfer.

Q059.L1t: American colleges use special names for students according to which year of study they are in.
Q059.L2t: The four traditional class-year names in US higher education are freshman, sophomore, junior, and senior, ordered from the first year to the last.
Q059.L3t: The second year of a four-year program comes after the first-year freshman stage and before the third and fourth years, and the term for it comes from Greek words meaning wise and foolish.
Q059.L4t: A second-year college student is usually called a sophomore.
Q059.L2f: The four class-year names in US colleges are always assigned by the student's age rather than by how many years they have completed.
Q059.L3f: In the standard four-year naming scheme, students are called by the third-year title once they have completed their first year and are in the middle of their second year.
Q059.L4f: A second-year college student is usually called a junior.

Q070.L1t: A quadratic function can model projectile motion, with a downward-opening parabola showing height changing over time.
Q070.L2t: The cannonball is above a given height exactly while the quadratic h(t) stays greater than that height, which is the interval between the two times it crosses that height.
Q070.L3t: Setting -4.9t^2 + 14t - 0.4 > 6 gives 4.9t^2 - 14t + 6.4 < 0, and the time above 6 meters is the gap between the two roots, which equals the square root of the discriminant divided by the leading coefficient, so sqrt(196 - 125.44)/4.9 = 8.4/4.9.
Q070.L4t: The cannonball stays above 6 meters for twelve sevenths of a second.
Q070.L2f: The cannonball's height follows a parabola that opens upward, so it dips to a minimum before rising again.
Q070.L3f: The time spent above 6 meters is the gap between the roots, and for this quadratic that gap works out to the discriminant 70.56 divided by 4.9 squared times 2, which comes to a little under one second.
Q070.L4f: The cannonball is above 6 meters for five sevenths of a second.

Q071.L1t: An equilateral triangle has three equal sides and three 60-degree angles, so its area can be found from the side length alone.
Q071.L2t: Dropping an altitude in an equilateral triangle splits it into two 30-60-90 right triangles, so the altitude is the side times the square root of 3 over 2.
Q071.L3t: The area is (sqrt(3)/4) times the side squared, so with a side of 12 it is (1.732/4) * 144, which is about 62.4.
Q071.L4t: The area is roughly sixty-two square inches.
Q071.L2f: The altitude of an equilateral triangle meets the base at a point one third of the way along it, splitting the triangle into two unequal right triangles.
Q071.L3f: The area of an equilateral triangle is about three quarters of the side squared, so for a side of 12 it is roughly 0.78 times 144.
Q071.L4f: The area is approximately 112 square inches.

Q072.L1t: Simplifying radical expressions with exponents relies on the laws of exponents, including rewriting roots as fractional powers.
Q072.L2t: A square root equals a power of one half, and multiplying powers of the same base adds their exponents while raising a power to a power multiplies them.
Q072.L3t: Since the square root of x^3 is x^(3/2), the product x * x^(3/2) is x^(5/2), and raising that to the fourth power multiplies the exponent by 4.
Q072.L4t: The simplified expression is x raised to the tenth power.
Q072.L2f: The square root of a power of x is found by doubling its exponent, so a radical always increases the exponent on x.
Q072.L3f: The lone x in front adds nothing to the exponent, and the radical of x^3 keeps its exponent of 3, so the base inside the parentheses is x^3 and only the fourth power remains to be applied.
Q072.L4f: The exponent of x in the simplified expression is twelve.

Q073.L1t: Composite functions and inverse functions are standard topics in algebra.
Q073.L2t: The composition f(g(x)) means applying g to x first and then applying f to the result.
Q073.L3t: Substituting g into f gives h(x)=3(2x-3)+4=6x-5, and the inverse comes from swapping x and y in y=6x-5 and solving for y.
Q073.L4t: The inverse of h is x plus 5, all divided by 6.
Q073.L2f: The composition f(g(x)) is defined by multiplying f(x) and g(x) together.
Q073.L3f: Composing the functions gives h(x)=3x+5, since the constant from g is simply replaced by the constant from f.

Q075.L1t: Ceiling and floor functions round real numbers to integers and often appear in problems about sums.

Q076.L1t: Congruence modulo 13 sorts every integer into one of 13 residue classes according to its remainder on division by 13.

Q076.L4f: The count of integers from -200 to 200 that are congruent to 5 mod 13 is thirty.

Q077.L1t: A circle's equation can be written either in general form or in center-radius form.

Q079.L1t: A week has seven days, so weekdays repeat in a fixed cycle that can be tracked with remainders after dividing by seven.

Q090.L1t: Predicate logic uses quantifiers, predicate letters and individual constants to formalize natural-language arguments.
Q090.L2t: The symbol ⊃ is the material conditional, and ~(∀x)~Wx is the negation of a universal claim about everything.
Q090.L3t: In the second premise the antecedent is being out to dinner and the consequent is not being at work, and the conclusion denies that everything is not at work.
Q090.L4t: The correct reading says lawyers who are out to dinner are not at work, and it concludes that not everything is not at work.
Q090.L2f: In symbolizations of this kind, predicate letters must always be capital letters taken from the end of the alphabet.
Q090.L3f: In the second premise the antecedent is not being at work and the consequent is being out to dinner, and the negated universal in the conclusion amounts to saying that everything is at work.
Q090.L4f: The best interpretation reads the second premise as saying lawyers who are not at work are out to dinner, and it concludes that not everything is at work.

Q091.L1t: An argument is made up of premises that are offered as support, together with a conclusion that those premises are meant to establish.
Q091.L2t: The passage traces genetics through three historical moments: the description of inheritance principles, the rediscovery of the laws of inheritance, and the later grasp of DNA's importance.
Q091.L3t: The dated facts about inheritance, rediscovery and DNA are all offered as evidence, with words like 'furthermore' and 'even then' marking them as added support for the opening claim about the field's age.
Q091.L4t: The conclusion is the claim that, historically speaking, genetics is a young science.
Q091.L2f: The molecular structure of DNA was first identified in the 1850s, long before the laws of inheritance were rediscovered.

Q091.L4f: The conclusion is that even after the rediscovery of the laws of inheritance, DNA's importance was not really understood until the 1950s.

Q092.L1t: Propositional logic symbolizes whole English sentences as formulas built from sentence letters and connectives such as negation, conjunction and disjunction.
Q092.L2t: In a symbolization, a single sentence letter can stand for a whole claim like "Everybody loves Raymond," and the phrase "or not" can be read as adding the negation of that claim.
Q092.L3t: The sentence offers the claim and its own negation as alternatives, so the right formula joins the letter and its negation with the connective that means "at least one of these holds."
Q092.L4t: The sentence is best symbolized as the letter disjoined with its negation, which is a tautology.
Q092.L2f: Sentence letters in propositional logic can only stand for single names such as Raymond, never for whole claims, and "or not" is always read as a conditional.
Q092.L3f: The phrase "or not" is just a tag that leaves the main claim unchanged, so the sentence asserts only that everybody loves Raymond and needs no connective at all.
Q092.L4f: The best symbolization is just the bare sentence letter L, asserting that everybody loves Raymond.

Q093.L1t: Conditional propositions in logic have two parts, an antecedent and a consequent, and English expresses them with many different connecting phrases.
Q093.L2t: The phrase "only if" is a standard English way of expressing a conditional, and it works differently from the word "if" alone.
Q093.L3t: In an "only if" sentence, the clause that comes before "only if" is the one that implies the clause after it, so the clause after it states a necessary condition and is the consequent.
Q093.L4t: The antecedent is the claim that the university raises tuition.
Q093.L2f: The phrase "only if" is a biconditional that makes the two clauses equivalent, so a conditional with "only if" has no separate antecedent.
Q093.L3f: In an "only if" sentence, the clause that follows the phrase is the one that implies the first clause, so the later conditions such as the trustees' recommendation come first in the conditional's order of implication.
Q093.L4f: The antecedent is the claim that the board of trustees recommends the tuition raise.

Q094.L1t: Predicate logic uses quantifiers, predicate letters and connectives to symbolize English statements about all or some members of a group.
Q094.L2t: Universal statements of the form "All A are B" are normally symbolized with a universal quantifier governing a single conditional, not a conjunction.
Q094.L3t: For "All A are B," the universal quantifier takes a conditional whose antecedent is the predicate of the subject class and whose consequent is the predicate attributed to it, so first-year students must go in the antecedent and the swim test taking in the consequent.
Q094.L4t: The best translation is the universal conditional whose antecedent says x is a first-year student and whose consequent says x takes a swim test.
Q094.L2f: Universal statements of the form "All A are B" are normally symbolized with a universal quantifier governing a disjunction of the two predicates.
Q094.L3f: A universal claim says that each thing has at least one of the two properties named, so "All A are B" is properly symbolized by joining the two predicates with inclusive disjunction.
Q094.L4f: The best translation is the universal quantification of a disjunction saying that everything is either a first-year student or takes a swim test.

Q095.L1t: Indirect truth tables test validity by assuming the premises are true and the conclusion false, and checking whether that assignment can be consistent.
Q095.L2t: A conditional like T ⊃ U is false only when T is true and U is false, so that is the only way this conclusion can fail.
Q095.L3t: Making the conclusion false requires T true and U false, which makes the first premise's antecedent true, so that premise forces W false, and the second premise then forces X true.
Q095.L4t: No assignment makes all four premises true and the conclusion false, so the argument is valid and has no counterexample.
Q095.L2f: An indirect truth table works by assuming the conclusion is true and the premises false, and then looking for a contradiction.
Q095.L3f: A conditional is true whenever its consequent is false, even if its antecedent is true, so the first premise is satisfied when W is true.
Q095.L4f: The argument is invalid, because the premises can all be true and the conclusion false when T, W and Z are true while U and X are false.

Q096.L1t: In predicate logic, names of individuals are written as lowercase constants and relations as capital letters followed by those constants.
Q096.L2t: The key given defines Txy as x teaches y, so the first letter after T names the teacher and the second names the one taught.
Q096.L3t: David is the one doing the teaching and Chris is the one being taught, so d must fill the first place after T and c the second.
Q096.L4t: The sentence is translated by putting the teacher d first and the student c second after T, giving Tdc.
Q096.L2f: Constants for individuals in predicate logic are written as capital letters, and a predicate letter is always written in lowercase.
Q096.L3f: In Txy the first letter after T names the one being taught and the second names the teacher.
Q096.L4f: David teaches Chris is best translated with c first and d second after T, so Chris is written as the teacher.

Q097.L1t: Categorical statements such as all, no, some and some-not are translated into predicate logic using quantifiers and predicate letters.
Q097.L2t: A universal negative of the form No A are B says that nothing is both an A and a B.
Q097.L3t: No artifacts are people means that for every x, if x is an artifact then x is not a person, so the universal quantifier governs a conditional with a negated consequent.
Q097.L4t: The statement is translated as a universally quantified conditional: for all x, if x is an artifact then x is not a person.
Q097.L2f: Universal negatives in predicate logic are normally expressed with an existential quantifier and a conjunction.
Q097.L3f: Lowercase letters such as p can stand for whole kinds like people, so a general claim about artifacts can be expressed as the negation of a predicate applied to that single term.
Q097.L4f: The best translation negates the artifact predicate applied to the constant standing for people, with no quantifier.

Q098.L1t: A truth table for an argument with three sentence letters has eight rows, one for each combination of truth values.
Q098.L2t: An argument is invalid exactly when some row makes every premise true and the conclusion false.
Q098.L3t: The second premise, a conjunction with a negated S, is true only when S is false and U is true, so only rows with those values can make all the premises true; check whether the conclusion fails in them.
Q098.L4t: The argument is invalid, because the row with S false, T false and U true makes all three premises true while the conclusion is false.
Q098.L2f: A truth table for three sentence letters needs only four rows, because the values of the third letter are fixed by the other two.
Q098.L3f: A negated letter is true when the letter itself is true, so the second premise is satisfied in rows where S and U are both true.
Q098.L4f: The argument is invalid, and the row with S and U true and T false is a counterexample.

Q099.L1t: Predicate logic translates English statements using quantifiers, predicate letters and truth-functional connectives.
Q099.L2t: In this translation R and A stand for the properties 'is a robot' and 'is an artifact', and the universal quantifier ranges over everything in the domain.
Q099.L3t: The sentence says that for anything at all, if it is a robot then it is an artifact, and it says nothing about non-robots, so a universal claim about a restricted class needs a conditional.
Q099.L4t: The sentence is correctly rendered as a universally quantified conditional with robot as the antecedent and artifact as the consequent.
Q099.L2f: In translations like this, predicate letters name particular individuals rather than standing for properties.
Q099.L3f: A universal claim says that everything in the domain has both properties, so the two predicates should be joined by conjunction under the quantifier.
Q099.L4f: The correct translation is the universally quantified conjunction of robot and artifact.

Q110.L1t: The free-electron model explains many of the electrical and thermal properties of metals.
Q110.L2t: Conduction electrons in a typical metal have Fermi energies of several electron volts, while kT at room temperature is only about 0.025 eV.
Q110.L3t: The Pauli exclusion principle allows at most one electron per quantum state, so filling states from the bottom up forces most electrons into high-energy states even at very low temperature.
Q110.L4t: Exclusion forces the electrons to fill states up to a high Fermi energy, forming a degenerate Fermi gas, so their mean kinetic energy far exceeds kT.
Q110.L2f: At room temperature the electronic heat capacity of a metal is roughly the classical value of 3/2 k per electron.
Q110.L3f: Conduction electrons in metals travel at speeds close to the speed of light, so relativistic kinetic energy dominates their motion.
Q110.L4f: Electrons in metals are highly relativistic, which is why their mean kinetic energy greatly exceeds kT.

Q111.L1t: In special relativity, observers in relative motion generally disagree about the time order and spacing of events.
Q111.L2t: Two events that are simultaneous in one frame but separated along the direction of motion are not simultaneous in a frame moving along that line.
Q111.L3t: The time offset seen by the moving observer is γvΔx/c², and 10 m corresponds to about 33 ns of light travel time, so γβ ≈ 13/33 ≈ 0.39, which gives β = γβ/√(1+(γβ)²).
Q111.L4t: The speed of O' relative to O is about 0.36 times the speed of light.
Q111.L2f: The time offset between two spatially separated events in a moving frame depends only on the observer's speed and not on how far apart the events are.
Q111.L3f: Because the moving observer's clocks also run slow, the measured 13 ns offset must be multiplied by γ twice, which forces the speed to be above half the speed of light.
Q111.L4f: The speed of O' relative to O is about 0.53 times the speed of light.

Q112.L1t: De Broglie's hypothesis extended wave-particle duality from light to matter.
Q112.L2t: Davisson and Germer's electron diffraction experiments confirmed that matter has wave properties.
Q112.L3t: For photons, p = h/λ, where h is the same constant that links photon energy to frequency in E = hf, and de Broglie proposed that this same relation holds for massive particles.
Q112.L4t: The constant linking a free particle's momentum and wavelength is the quantum of action that appears in E = hf, Planck's constant.
Q112.L2f: De Broglie published his hypothesis in 1905, and it was first verified by observing the photoelectric effect.
Q112.L3f: De Broglie obtained matter wavelengths by building on hydrogen's spectral-series constant, so that constant is what ties a particle's momentum to its wavelength.
Q112.L4f: The constant relating a free particle's momentum and wavelength is the Rydberg constant.

Q113.L1t: Hydrogen energy levels are labeled by the quantum numbers n and l, with l running from 0 to n−1.
Q113.L2t: Electric dipole transitions in hydrogen are restricted by selection rules on the orbital angular momentum quantum number.
Q113.L3t: The emitted photon carries one unit of angular momentum, so l must change by exactly one, which means a state with l = 1 can only go to l = 0 or l = 2.
Q113.L4t: The transition to n = 3, l = 1 is forbidden because l does not change.
Q113.L2f: In an allowed hydrogen transition the principal quantum number n must always change by exactly one.
Q113.L3f: The selection rule says l can stay the same or increase but never decrease in a transition.
Q113.L4f: The transition to n = 3, l = 0 is the one that cannot be reached by an allowed transition.

Q114.L1t: Semiconductors are materials whose conductivity lies between that of metals and insulators and can be tuned by adding impurity atoms.
Q114.L2t: Doping adds donor or acceptor atoms that supply extra electrons or holes, which changes the carrier concentration and the conductivity of the material.
Q114.L3t: When current flows through a conductor in a transverse magnetic field, the Lorentz force pushes the moving carriers sideways, building a transverse voltage whose polarity depends on whether the carriers are positive or negative.
Q114.L4t: The sign of the carriers is found by measuring the transverse voltage-based coefficient that appears when current flows in a magnetic field, namely the Hall coefficient.
Q114.L2f: In a doped semiconductor, the carrier concentration is fixed by temperature alone and is unaffected by the density of donor or acceptor impurities.
Q114.L3f: The response of a material to an applied magnetic field, whether it is attracted or repelled, switches sign directly with the sign of the mobile charge carriers, so it reveals their sign.
Q114.L4f: The sign of the carriers is revealed by measuring how the material responds to an applied magnetic field in terms of its magnetic susceptibility.

Q115.L1t: Special relativity predicts that lengths measured along the direction of relative motion differ from lengths measured in the object's rest frame.
Q115.L2t: Length contraction applies only to the dimension parallel to the relative velocity, and the rest length is the longest length any observer can measure.
Q115.L3t: The contracted length equals the rest length times the square root of one minus v squared over c squared, so a ratio of 0.80 requires the square root term to equal 0.80, which means v²/c² = 0.36.
Q115.L4t: The observer must move at six-tenths of the speed of light.
Q115.L2f: Length contraction in special relativity affects dimensions perpendicular to the motion as well as the parallel one, and the rest length is the shortest length any observer can measure.
Q115.L3f: The contracted length equals the rest length times the square root of one minus v squared over c squared, and a ratio of 0.80 is obtained when v²/c² = 0.75, so the speed is lower than most would expect.
Q115.L4f: The observer must move at half the speed of light, which is the speed that shortens the rod to 0.80 m.

Q116.L1t: The cosmic microwave background is thermal radiation left over from the early universe, and it has cooled as the universe has expanded.
Q116.L2t: The CMB has a blackbody spectrum, and its temperature today is measured to be about 2.7 K.
Q116.L3t: The temperature of the background radiation is inversely proportional to the scale factor of the universe, so a fourfold higher temperature (12 K versus 3 K) corresponds to a scale factor four times smaller.
Q116.L4t: At 12 K, typical separations between galaxies were one-quarter of what they are today.
Q116.L2f: The CMB was emitted by hot stars in the first galaxies, and its spectrum is not a blackbody, so it has no simple relation to the universe's expansion.
Q116.L3f: The radiation temperature is directly proportional to the scale factor of the universe, so a fourfold higher temperature means the universe was four times larger, and distances between galaxies were correspondingly greater.
Q116.L4f: At 12 K, typical galaxies were separated by twice the distances we see today, since the universe has contracted as it cooled.

Q117.L1t: Special relativity says that lengths and time intervals measured in one frame differ from those measured in a frame moving relative to it.
Q117.L2t: The length of an object along its direction of motion is measured to be shorter by the factor 1/γ, where γ = 1/√(1−v²/c²), compared with its rest length.
Q117.L3t: At 0.8c the Lorentz factor is 5/3, so the observer sees a stick 0.6 m long, and the passing time is this contracted length divided by the speed 0.8c.
Q117.L4t: The stick takes about 2.5 nanoseconds to pass the observer.
Q117.L2f: A moving object's length along its direction of motion is measured to be longer than its rest length by the factor γ.
Q117.L3f: The observer must apply the 0.6 contraction factor twice, once to shorten the stick and again to shorten the passing time, which gives a much smaller time.
Q117.L4f: The stick takes about 1.6 nanoseconds to pass the observer.

Q118.L1t: Capacitors store charge and energy, and combining them in series or parallel changes the effective capacitance of the circuit.

Q118.L3t: Two identical capacitors in series act as half a capacitor, and when this pair is joined in parallel with the first, the original charge CV₀ is shared across a total capacitance of 3C/2 at one common voltage.

Q118.L4f: The final voltage on the first capacitor is one-fifth of its initial voltage.

Q119.L1t: When fast electrons strike a metal target they lose energy in several ways, producing both a continuous X-ray spectrum and discrete spectral lines.

Q180.L1t: Photographs offered at trial are a form of demonstrative or real evidence that must be authenticated before a court admits them.
Q180.L2t: Authentication of a photograph does not require that the person who took it testify, because any witness with knowledge of the scene may authenticate it.
Q180.L3t: A photograph is authenticated by testimony from a witness with knowledge that it is a fair and accurate representation of the subject it depicts, and the photographer here only identified the prints as the ones she took and gave to the owner.
Q180.L4t: The photographs should be excluded because no witness testified that they fairly and accurately show the ruptured tank.
Q180.L2f: Photographs can be authenticated only by the person who operated the camera, and no other witness with knowledge of the scene may do so.
Q180.L3f: Photographs are admissible only if the proponent shows an unbroken chain of custody for the film from the moment it was shot until it was developed, much as with physical evidence like drugs.
Q180.L4f: The photographs should be excluded because there was an unaccountable gap in the chain of custody between the taking of the photographs and the processing of the negatives.

Q181.L1t: Employment contracts are governed by general contract law, and courts review their terms individually for enforceability.
Q181.L2t: An at-will employment arrangement can be replaced by a written agreement that sets new terms, including a notice period for termination.
Q181.L3t: A clause that restricts competition after employment ends is enforceable only if it is reasonable in duration and geographic scope, and a bar on any aspect of the hardware business for two years across a 50-mile radius reaches further than the employer's legitimate interest in protecting its business.
Q181.L4t: The salary and the 60-day termination provisions would be enforced, but the covenant not to compete would not be enforced as written.
Q181.L2f: A written employment agreement signed after the employee has already worked for the employer is void for lack of any new consideration.
Q181.L3f: A court will enforce a non-compete covenant of any length and geographic reach so long as the employee signed it, and the only term likely to be struck down is the fixed $1,500 sum payable on breach.
Q181.L4f: The agreement would be enforced in full except for the $1,500 payment clause, which would be struck as an unenforceable penalty.

Q182.L1t: Future interests in land, such as remainders and reversions, are governed by common law rules on their creation, classification and transfer.
Q182.L2t: At common law the Rule Against Perpetuities voids a contingent interest that might vest more than twenty-one years after the lives in being at its creation.
Q182.L3t: The remainder to the neighbor and her heirs was given to an ascertained, living person with no condition precedent, so it was vested at creation, and a vested remainder is not subject to the Rule and passes by will when its holder dies.
Q182.L4t: The friend holds only a life estate, and the remainder passed under the neighbor's will to the charity as a vested remainder.
Q182.L2f: The woman's conveyance to the friend for life created a life estate that could be transferred to others only with the consent of the remainderman.
Q182.L3f: The remainder to the neighbor and her heirs was contingent because the heirs could not be known until her death, so it could vest too remotely and was therefore invalid under the Rule Against Perpetuities.
Q182.L4f: The friend holds a life estate and the woman keeps a reversion, because the neighbor's remainder is void under the Rule Against Perpetuities.

Q183.L1t: Trespass to land is an intentional tort protecting a possessor's interest in exclusive use of their land.
Q183.L2t: Liability for trespass requires that the defendant's act or the thing they set in motion physically invade another's land, and that the invasion be either intended or the result of negligence or an abnormally dangerous activity.
Q183.L3t: The homeowner did not intend the mower to enter the neighbor's land, and he neither knew nor could have discovered the defect by any feasible inspection, so he was not negligent, and operating a riding mower is not an abnormally dangerous activity.
Q183.L4t: The neighbor will not prevail, because the homeowner neither intended the entry nor was at fault, since the defect could not have been found by any reasonable inspection.
Q183.L2f: Trespass to land is a tort that historically required the plaintiff to prove actual physical harm to the property before any claim could be brought.
Q183.L3f: Trespass to land is a strict-liability tort in which the defendant's intent, knowledge and fault are irrelevant, so any physical object that comes onto another's land creates liability for the person who owns it.
Q183.L4f: The neighbor will prevail, because the mower physically came onto the neighbor's land and that entry alone makes the homeowner liable for trespass.

Q184.L1t: The Dead Man's Statute is a rule of evidence that, in some jurisdictions, limits testimony about dealings with a deceased person.
Q184.L2t: Dead Man's Statutes typically disqualify only interested parties, such as those with a stake in the outcome of the suit, from testifying about transactions or communications with the decedent.
Q184.L3t: The clerk is a disinterested third party with no stake in the estate, and he is testifying to what he personally saw the testator write in the hotel register, so the statute's bar on interested witnesses does not reach him.
Q184.L4t: The testimony should be admitted, because the clerk has personal knowledge of what he observed and is not an interested party barred by the Dead Man's Statute.
Q184.L2f: The hotel register entries were made years before the testator died, and registers of this kind are generally kept in a guest's own handwriting.
Q184.L3f: Dead Man's Statutes in most jurisdictions bar any witness, interested or not, from testifying about the decedent's statements or conduct once the decedent has died and the claim is against the estate.
Q184.L4f: The testimony should be excluded, because the Dead Man's Statute bars testimony about the deceased testator's conduct in a claim against his estate.

Q185.L1t: Contract modifications are governed by the Uniform Commercial Code when the contract is for the sale of goods.
Q185.L2t: Under the UCC, a good-faith modification of a contract for the sale of goods needs no consideration to be binding.
Q185.L3t: Under the UCC, a contract for the sale of goods at a price of $500 or more must be in writing, and a modification that brings the contract within the statute of frauds must also be in writing, and the modified contract here is for 800 gidgets at a price of $3,200.
Q185.L4t: The modification is probably unenforceable because it was made only orally and the resulting contract is for goods priced at $500 or more, so it fails the statute of frauds.
Q185.L2f: Gidgets are sold by quantity rather than by unique specification, which makes them fungible goods that are easy to substitute on the market.
Q185.L3f: The parol evidence rule bars evidence of any later oral agreement that contradicts the terms of a fully integrated written contract, even if the oral agreement was made after the writing was signed.
Q185.L4f: The modification is probably unenforceable because the parol evidence rule bars the oral change that contradicts the quantity term in the written contract.

Q186.L1t: Tort law allows a plaintiff to establish negligence through direct evidence or, in some cases, through circumstantial evidence.
Q186.L2t: The doctrine of res ipsa loquitur lets a jury infer negligence from the nature of an accident, and it applies to some elevator falls.
Q186.L3t: Res ipsa loquitur permits an inference of negligence when the harmful instrumentality was in the defendant's exclusive control and the event is of a kind that ordinarily does not happen without negligence, and a free-falling elevator fits both elements.
Q186.L4t: The judge will not dismiss the case, because the circumstances of the elevator's fall allow the jury to infer the owner's negligence.
Q186.L2f: Res ipsa loquitur is a rule that applies only to accidents caused by defective products and never to a building's equipment.
Q186.L3f: A plaintiff in a negligence case must always produce specific direct evidence of what the defendant did wrong, and an unexplained accident is never enough to reach a jury.
Q186.L4f: The judge will dismiss the case, because the plaintiff always carries the burden of proving negligence and has offered no evidence of it beyond the accident itself.

Q187.L1t: Accomplice liability and facilitation offenses are part of criminal law, and they turn on the defendant's mental state and conduct.

Q187.L4f: Criminal liability is least likely for the hotel clerk who knew a guest was using her room for prostitution.

Q188.L1t: Property law allows landowners to limit how land is used through private agreements, and these agreements are subject to rules on enforceability.
